content: Chronic cold urticaria, also referred to as cold allergy or cold hives, is a condition in which an individual develops an allergic reaction to cold temperatures. When exposed to cold environments or cold water, affected individuals may experience redness, itching, swelling, and hives on their skin. In severe cases, exposure to cold water, such as swimming, can provoke life-threatening reactions, including fainting, shock, or even death. Symptoms of Chronic Cold Urticaria Symptoms typically manifest when individuals are exposed to cold water or a sudden drop in temperature. While most reactions occur at temperatures of 40°F (4°C) or lower, symptoms may worsen as the skin rewarms after exposure. Damp and windy conditions are more likely to trigger cold urticaria. The severity of symptoms varies widely among individuals. Some may experience mild reactions, while others may suffer from severe and systemic symptoms. The duration of the condition is unpredictable; for some, it resolves within months, while others may endure symptoms for years. Common symptoms include: Red, itchy hives that appear after cold exposure and typically last about 30 minutes. Swelling of the hands when holding cold objects. Swelling of the lips after consuming cold foods. In severe cases, swelling of the tongue and throat, which can obstruct breathing. While some individuals experience localized symptoms, others may develop systemic reactions, such as: Fainting. Chills. A rapid heart rate. Swelling of the arms, legs, or torso. Severe Reactions Exposure to cold can be particularly dangerous for individuals with cold urticaria, especially during activities like swimming, which exposes large areas of skin to cold water. This can lead to the release of high levels of histamine and other immune system chemicals, causing a significant drop in blood pressure. This may result in fainting, shock, or, in rare cases, death. Loss of consciousness due to cold exposure while swimming can increase the risk of drowning. Causes of Chronic Cold Urticaria The exact cause of cold urticaria is not well understood. However, it is believed that some individuals have hypersensitive skin cells that overreact to cold stimuli. This hypersensitivity may be due to inherited traits or underlying illnesses, such as viral infections. Cold exposure triggers an immune response, leading to the release of histamine and other chemicals, which cause symptoms like itching, redness, and swelling. Risk Factors Cold urticaria can affect individuals of any age or gender, but certain groups are at higher risk: Children and young adults: This population often experiences primary acquired urticaria, which typically resolves within two to three years without treatment. Recent viral infections: Individuals recovering from infections like mycoplasma pneumonia or mononucleosis may develop cold urticaria. Underlying health conditions: Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, hepatitis, or cancer can predispose individuals to secondary acquired urticaria, which is less common. Inherited traits: Rarely, individuals may inherit familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, which causes painful, itchy hives and flu-like symptoms after cold exposure. When to Seek Medical Attention Immediate medical care is necessary if severe reactions occur after sudden cold exposure, such as: Feeling lightheaded. Difficulty breathing. Swelling of the throat. For mild skin reactions, consult a doctor to rule out any underlying conditions contributing to the symptoms. Diagnosis Cold urticaria is diagnosed by placing an ice cube on the skin for several minutes. If a raised, red bump (hive) forms after the ice is removed, the diagnosis is confirmed. Most cases are seen in children and young adults, often without an apparent cause. Symptoms typically improve and resolve within weeks to months, though some individuals may experience symptoms for years. Rarely, underlying immune system conditions, such as hepatitis, rheumatoid arthritis, cancer, or infections like mononucleosis, may be responsible. Treatment Options While there is no cure for cold urticaria, treatment can help manage symptoms. This includes avoiding cold temperatures and sudden temperature changes. Medications can also help prevent and reduce symptoms. Common treatments include: Antihistamines: These block the release of histamine, alleviating symptoms like itching. Examples include: Loratadine (Claritin) Fexofenadine (Allegra) Cetirizine (Zyrtec) Levocetirizine (Xyzal) Desloratadine (Clarinex) Cyproheptadine: This antihistamine affects nerve impulses that contribute to cold urticaria symptoms. Doxepin (Sinequan): Primarily used to treat anxiety and depression, this medication can also reduce cold urticaria symptoms. While these medications can ease symptoms, they do not cure the condition. Additionally, they may not address underlying health conditions causing cold urticaria. Consult a physician for proper evaluation and treatment. Prognosis For most individuals, symptoms of cold urticaria resolve within weeks to months. However, some may experience symptoms for several years. Complications The primary complication of cold urticaria is a severe reaction following extensive skin exposure to cold, such as swimming in cold water. Prevention Preventing cold urticaria is not possible. However, once symptoms appear, taking prescribed medications and avoiding cold exposure to unprotected skin can help manage and prevent symptoms.
